items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ethical dilemma"?
options: A situation in which ethical principles or obligations conflict, so any action involves costs
Legal obligations in some contexts to report certain information (e.g. child abuse) to authorities, which may conflict with confidentiality
Jean Rouch's approach of showing films to participants and including their responses, making them collaborators
Informed agreement to participate in research conducted on digital platforms, complicated by public/private ambiguity and pseudonymous identities
items.answer: A situation in which ethical principles or obligations conflict, so any action involves costs
items.markingKey: A. "ethical dilemma" is a situation in which ethical principles or obligations conflict, so any action involves costs.

items.stem: Explain why ethical issues in ethnography are often more complex than in laboratory research.
items.answer: Ethnography involves long-term personal relationships, changing topics, unpredictable events and publication about real communities, so consent, harm and confidentiality must be negotiated continually.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ethnography involves long-term personal relationships, changing topics, unpredictable events and publication about real communities, so consent, harm and confidentiality must be negotiated continually. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Anonymity is always what participants want." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Some participants want recognition or credit for their knowledge, and Indigenous communities may want to be named; anonymity must be negotiated.
items.markingKey: Some participants want recognition or credit for their knowledge, and Indigenous communities may want to be named; anonymity must be negotiated. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Chagnon's Yanomamö: The Fierce People (among Yanomami communities of southern Venezuela and northern Brazil (fieldwork from 1964)) as your example, describe how social relations is shown.
items.answer: The controversy after Patrick Tierney's Darkness in El Dorado (2000) raised questions about gifts of steel tools, consent to the 1960s blood sampling, and the anthropologist's effect on relations between villages.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The controversy after Patrick Tierney's Darkness in El Dorado (2000) raised questions about gifts of steel tools, consent to the 1960s blood sampling, and the anthropologist's effect on relations between villages. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Napoleon Chagnon, Yanomamö: The Fierce People (1968), among Yanomami communities of southern Venezuela and northern Brazil (fieldwork from 1964)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to social relations. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

For two years I volunteered at the night shelter, where I also conducted my research. Most residents knew me as "the student who helps". Pete, who has been sleeping rough for eight years, told me about selling his medication to buy alcohol, then added, "But that's just between us." The shelter manager later asked me for "any information that would help us support the residents better". The council, which funds the shelter, has proposed excluding residents who misuse medication.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a homeless shelter in the United Kingdom.

Explain why the researcher's dual role creates ethical difficulties, using one or more anthropological concepts. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: As a volunteer, residents may not see the researcher as a researcher, so consent is unclear; Pete's confidence and the manager's request create a conflict between confidentiality and the institution's interests; the council policy means disclosure could cause serious harm (exclusion), so obligations to participants, the shelter and funders compete.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: As a volunteer, residents may not see the researcher as a researcher, so consent is unclear; Pete's confidence and the manager's request create a conflict between confidentiality and the institution's interests; the council policy means disclosure could cause serious harm (exclusion), so obligations to participants, the shelter and funders compete. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: With reference to Holmes's border crossing, explain how it illustrates risk and inequality in participation.
items.answer: Holmes crossed the border illegally with Triqui companions to understand their experience and was briefly jailed. His US citizenship meant his consequences were mild while his companions were deported, raising questions about the ethics of sharing risks unequally.
items.markingKey: Context (Holmes crossed the border illegally with Triqui companions to understand their experience and was briefly jailed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: his US citizenship meant his consequences were mild while his companions were deported, raising questions about the ethics of sharing risks unequally. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to risk and inequality in participation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the benefits of covert research can outweigh its ethical costs. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Covert research may be justified only exceptionally, when harm is serious, participants are powerful wrongdoers and no overt method exists.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: exposing organ trafficking or abuse may protect vulnerable people; some powerful actors will never consent; deception breaches trust and consent; it damages access for future researchers; risks to the researcher and participants. Suitable ethnographies include Bourgois's In Search of Respect, Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping, Chagnon's Yanomamö: The Fierce People. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The AAA's first principle: avoid physical, psychological, social, legal or economic harm to participants and communities"?
options: do no harm
digital footprint
data protection
online consent
items.answer: do no harm
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of do no harm.

items.stem: Explain why anthropologists may face conflicts between honesty and protecting participants.
items.answer: Accurate description may reveal illegal, stigmatised or embarrassing practices, so anthropologists must decide what to omit or disguise without distorting their findings.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Accurate description may reveal illegal, stigmatised or embarrassing practices, so anthropologists must decide what to omit or disguise without distorting their findings. items.stem: Explain the difference between confidentiality and mandatory reporting.
items.answer: Confidentiality is the promise not to share participants' information; mandatory reporting is a legal duty to disclose certain information (e.g. child abuse), so the two can conflict.
items.markingKey: Confidentiality is the promise not to share participants' information; mandatory reporting is a legal duty to disclose certain information (e.g. child abuse), so the two can conflict. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "applied anthropology"?
options: The use of anthropological knowledge and methods to address practical problems in health, development, business, education or policy
Informed agreement to participate in research conducted on digital platforms, complicated by public/private ambiguity and pseudonymous identities
The study of, and work within, programmes intended to improve living standards, including critical analysis of development itself
The use of photography, film and other media in research, and the study of visual culture
items.answer: The use of anthropological knowledge and methods to address practical problems in health, development, business, education or policy
items.markingKey: A. "applied anthropology" is the use of anthropological knowledge and methods to address practical problems in health, development, business, education or policy.

items.stem: Explain why corporate anthropology raises ethical questions.
items.answer: Research may serve company profits over participants' interests, findings may be proprietary and unpublished, and participants may not understand how their data are used.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Research may serve company profits over participants' interests, findings may be proprietary and unpublished, and participants may not understand how their data are used. items.answer: Applied work uses the same methods and often produces important insights; the main differences are purpose, timescale and audience.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The consultancy hired me to find out why farmers were not using the new weather app. On the first day, the project manager said: "We need a slide that says what features to add." In the village, I learned that farmers trusted the forecast of an elderly woman, Mama Neema, who read the movement of ants, and that most phones were shared by several households and owned by men. When I presented this, the manager asked whether we could "build Mama Neema into the app". The farmers' cooperative has asked to see my report; the contract says it belongs to the company.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an applied research project in rural Tanzania.

With reference to the concept of power, analyse what the text shows about the opportunities and ethical problems of corporate applied anthropology. Make clear which key concept you are using and why it is relevant.
items.answer: Ethnography revealed social reasons for low uptake (trust in local knowledge, gendered phone ownership) that a technical approach missed – showing applied value. But the company wants simple product features, may appropriate local knowledge (Mama Neema) and owns the report, so participants cannot access findings; this raises issues of ownership, benefit-sharing and representation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Ethnography revealed social reasons for low uptake (trust in local knowledge, gendered phone ownership) that a technical approach missed – showing applied value. But the company wants simple product features, may appropriate local knowledge (Mama Neema) and owns the report, so participants cannot access findings; this raises issues of ownership, benefit-sharing and representation. items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Ferguson's The Anti-Politics Machine and Richards's Ebola, compare and contrast the role of power in applied and public anthropology: advocacy, development and corporate work.
items.answer: Ferguson's The Anti-Politics Machine (on the World Bank–supported Thaba-Tseka development project in Lesotho (1975–1984)): Development discourse portrayed Lesotho as an isolated farming economy needing technical fixes, ignoring its role as a labour reserve for South African mines; the project failed but expanded state bureaucratic power. Richards's Ebola (in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2015 West African Ebola epidemic): Top-down responses that ignored local knowledge produced distrust, while co-operation with chiefs and communities proved more effective. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Distinguish between applied anthropology and academic anthropology.
items.answer: Applied anthropology addresses practical problems for clients or communities; academic anthropology mainly seeks to produce theoretical and descriptive knowledge for scholarship. The boundary is increasingly blurred.
items.markingKey: Applied anthropology addresses practical problems for clients or communities; academic anthropology mainly seeks to produce theoretical and descriptive knowledge for scholarship. The boundary is increasingly blurred. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between anthropology for development and anthropology of development.
items.answer: Anthropology of development critically studies development institutions and discourses (Ferguson); anthropology for development works within projects to improve them.
items.markingKey: Anthropology of development critically studies development institutions and discourses (Ferguson); anthropology for development works within projects to improve them. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "digital footprint"?
options: Jean Rouch's approach of showing films to participants and including their responses, making them collaborators
The AAA's first principle: avoid physical, psychological, social, legal or economic harm to participants and communities
The traceable data a person leaves online, which can make quoted posts identifiable even when names are removed
Secure storage, anonymisation and limited sharing of research data, including field notes, recordings and photographs
items.answer: The traceable data a person leaves online, which can make quoted posts identifiable even when names are removed
items.markingKey: C. "digital footprint" is the traceable data a person leaves online, which can make quoted posts identifiable even when names are removed.

items.stem: Explain the difference between private online data and public online data.
items.answer: Public data are accessible to anyone (open posts); private data are restricted to members (closed groups, messages). Ethical use of both requires attention to users' expectations.
items.markingKey: Public data are accessible to anyone (open posts); private data are restricted to members (closed groups, messages). Ethical use of both requires attention to users' expectations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the text below.

I joined the online forum for young people with diabetes as part of my research. Members post photographs of their glucose readings and, sometimes, of their bodies after injections. The forum is public, but the rules say "This is a safe space". When I posted to explain my research, one member, @sugarbaby, replied: "Cool, but don't screenshot us." Another sent me a private message asking me to "tell the doctors what it's really like". The forum moderator asked for my university's ethics approval letter.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an online health forum.

Using the key concept of identity, explain why the forum is an ethically complex research site. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: The forum is technically public but defined by members as a "safe space", so expectations of privacy conflict with access; members are young and share health information and body images (sensitive data); responses range from conditional consent ("don't screenshot") to a request for advocacy, and the moderator acts as a gatekeeper.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The forum is technically public but defined by members as a "safe space", so expectations of privacy conflict with access; members are young and share health information and body images (sensitive data); responses range from conditional consent ("don't screenshot") to a request for advocacy, and the moderator acts as a gatekeeper. items.stem: With reference to one ethnography you have studied, for example the Why We Post project, explain the relevance of materiality to the ethics of digital and visual anthropology.
items.answer: Social media are treated as places where people live, not just technologies, and what people post varies sharply from site to site.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Social media are treated as places where people live, not just technologies, and what people post varies sharply from site to site. Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Refer to specific situations in the text rather than listing general principles.

items.stem: Explain why visual images raise particular ethical issues in anthropology.
items.answer: Images make people identifiable, can be circulated beyond the original context, may be edited to create a misleading narrative and can exoticise; consent for each use and audience is needed.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A film or photograph shows the truth more directly than writing." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Images are selected, framed, edited and narrated, so they are constructions like texts (e.g. Gardner's narration in Dead Birds).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Gardner's Dead Birds (1964) shows representation in visual anthropology.
items.answer: Gardner's voiceover described the thoughts and feelings of Dani individuals and framed ritual warfare as central to Dani life. The narration imposed an outsider's interpretation, raising questions about who speaks for the people filmed.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that digital ethnography raises more serious ethical problems than traditional fieldwork? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Digital research intensifies some risks (traceability, scale) but the core ethical principles are the same.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: data are permanent, searchable and easily shared; consent is hard to obtain from large or anonymous groups; traditional fieldwork also raises consent and harm issues; digital methods can be anonymised and consent negotiated with communities. items.stem: Using Ferguson's study of the Thaba-Tseka project as an example, explain critical anthropology of development.
items.answer: Planners treated Lesotho as an isolated farming economy, but most rural income came from migrant work in South African mines; the agricultural project failed while a new district administration was built. Development's real effect was to expand bureaucratic state power and depoliticise poverty.

items.stem: Compare and contrast how power is shown in Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013) and Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995).
items.answer: Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies (with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005)): Holmes uses Bourdieu's idea of symbolic violence to show how this hierarchy is naturalised: supervisors, doctors and sometimes workers themselves explain Triqui suffering by their bodies or culture rather than by labour conditions. Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)): Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. items.stem:
Read the text below.

The consultancy hired me to find out why farmers were not using the new weather app. On the first day, the project manager said: "We need a slide that says what features to add." In the village, I learned that farmers trusted the forecast of an elderly woman, Mama Neema, who read the movement of ants, and that most phones were shared by several households and owned by men. When I presented this, the manager asked whether we could "build Mama Neema into the app". The farmers' cooperative has asked to see my report; the contract says it belongs to the company.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an applied research project in rural Tanzania.

With reference to power, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Richards's Ebola. Keep the comparison running throughout rather than treating each case separately.
items.answer: Text: Ethnography revealed social reasons for low uptake (trust in local knowledge, gendered phone ownership) that a technical approach missed – showing applied value. But the company wants simple product features, may appropriate local knowledge (Mama Neema) and owns the report, so participants cannot access findings; this raises issues of ownership, benefit-sharing and representation. Ethnography – Paul Richards, Ebola: How a People's Science Helped End an Epidemic (2016), in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2015 West African Ebola epidemic: Top-down responses that ignored local knowledge produced distrust, while co-operation with chiefs and communities proved more effective. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

For two years I volunteered at the night shelter, where I also conducted my research. Most residents knew me as "the student who helps". Pete, who has been sleeping rough for eight years, told me about selling his medication to buy alcohol, then added, "But that's just between us." The shelter manager later asked me for "any information that would help us support the residents better". The council, which funds the shelter, has proposed excluding residents who misuse medication.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a homeless shelter in the United Kingdom.

Using the key concept of social relations, explain why the researcher's dual role creates ethical difficulties. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: As a volunteer, residents may not see the researcher as a researcher, so consent is unclear; Pete's confidence and the manager's request create a conflict between confidentiality and the institution's interests; the council policy means disclosure could cause serious harm (exclusion), so obligations to participants, the shelter and funders compete.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Anthropologists should work within development and corporate organisations rather than criticise them from outside."
items.answer: Both roles are valuable; insiders need independence and transparency, and critics need engagement with practice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: inside influence can improve projects and products (Suchman, Ebola response); critique alone may not help communities. Arguments against: insiders may be co-opted or restricted by clients; independent critique exposes harms (Ferguson). Supported judgement: Both roles are valuable; insiders need independence and transparency, and critics need engagement with practice.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

I joined the online forum for young people with diabetes as part of my research. Members post photographs of their glucose readings and, sometimes, of their bodies after injections. The forum is public, but the rules say "This is a safe space". When I posted to explain my research, one member, @sugarbaby, replied: "Cool, but don't screenshot us." Another sent me a private message asking me to "tell the doctors what it's really like". The forum moderator asked for my university's ethics approval letter.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an online health forum.

With reference to identity, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Boellstorff's Coming of Age in Second Life. Make sure you contextualise the ethnography: author, people, place and time.
items.answer: Text: The forum is technically public but defined by members as a "safe space", so expectations of privacy conflict with access; members are young and share health information and body images (sensitive data); responses range from conditional consent ("don't screenshot") to a request for advocacy, and the moderator acts as a gatekeeper. Ethnography – Tom Boellstorff, Coming of Age in Second Life: An Anthropologist Explores the Virtually Human (2008), through participant observation inside the virtual world Second Life, conducted via his avatar (2004–2006): Residents created avatars and virtual selves, showing identity to be crafted and performed in virtual space. Comparison: similarities and differences in how identity is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Text: The forum is technically public but defined by members as a "safe space", so expectations of privacy conflict with access; members are young and share health information and body images (sensitive data); responses range from conditional consent ("don't screenshot") to a request for advocacy, and the moderator acts as a gatekeeper. Ethnography – Tom Boellstorff, Coming of Age in Second Life: An Anthropologist Explores the Virtually Human (2008), through participant observation inside the virtual world Second Life, conducted via his avatar (2004–2006): Residents created avatars and virtual selves, showing identity to be crafted and performed in virtual space. Comparison: similarities and differences in how identity is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them. Any well-contextualised ethnography is acceptable. Markbands – 9–10: sustained, insightful comparison of similarities and differences; ethnography fully contextualised; concepts and theory used critically; 7–8: detailed, accurate ethnographic knowledge; developed comparison of similarities and differences linked to key concepts; 5–6: relevant, contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time); explicit comparison with some analysis of similarities and differences; 3–4: some relevant ethnographic knowledge; mostly descriptive, the text and the ethnography treated separately; 1–2: limited knowledge; comparison implicit or absent; little reference to the text or to an ethnography; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Respond to the big question "Can an anthropologist ever fully understand another way of life?" by drawing on evaluating ethical issues in ethnographic research, the concept of power and Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013) or another ethnography.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies power explicitly and uses ethnography: Holmes uses Bourdieu's idea of symbolic violence to show how this hierarchy is naturalised: supervisors, doctors and sometimes workers themselves explain Triqui suffering by their bodies or culture rather than by labour conditions. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion. Markbands – 9–10: perceptive, well-argued response integrating key concepts, ethnography and theory, with a reasoned conclusion; 7–8: clear argument that applies the key concept to ethnographic material and considers more than one perspective; 5–6: relevant response using a key concept and an ethnography, with some analysis; 3–4: some relevant ideas; ethnographic or conceptual support is thin or general; 1–2: limited response to the big question; assertions with little anthropological support; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The consultancy hired me to find out why farmers were not using the new weather app. On the first day, the project manager said: "We need a slide that says what features to add." In the village, I learned that farmers trusted the forecast of an elderly woman, Mama Neema, who read the movement of ants, and that most phones were shared by several households and owned by men. When I presented this, the manager asked whether we could "build Mama Neema into the app". The farmers' cooperative has asked to see my report; the contract says it belongs to the company.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an applied research project in rural Tanzania.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. You may refer to ethical codes, but apply them to the situation described.
items.answer: Mama Neema's knowledge could be appropriated without consent or benefit; the community cannot access the report; the anthropologist should negotiate sharing of findings, protect individuals and be transparent with farmers about the commercial purpose. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people. Markbands – 9–10: insightful, balanced discussion of ethical dilemmas, competing obligations and possible responses, fully grounded in the text and professional codes; 7–8: well-developed discussion of several ethical issues and competing obligations, closely linked to the text; 5–6: relevant ethical issues explained with reference to the text and to professional principles; 3–4: some relevant ethical issues (e.g. consent, harm) identified and partly explained with reference to the text; 1–2: ethical issues identified only in general terms, with little reference to the text; 0: does not reach the standard described below.
